name: Komodo National Park & Flores
tagline: Wild Komodo dragons, pink sand beaches and dramatic island viewpoints, reached by boat from the harbour town of Labuan Bajo.
highlight: Standing on Padar Island's viewpoint at sunrise, three curved bays of black, white and pink sand spreading out below in every direction.
shortDescription: A dramatic island region in eastern Indonesia, home to wild Komodo dragons, pink sand beaches and some of the country's best diving.
metaDescription: A Komodo National Park and Flores travel guide: wild Komodo dragons, Padar Island, Pink Beach, Kelimutu's crater lakes and how to plan a Labuan Bajo trip.
knownFor: Wild Komodo dragons, pink sand beaches, island-hopping
budget: Rp 600,000–1,800,000 per day, plus boat tour costs

intro: Komodo National Park is one of Indonesia's most dramatic corners, a scatter of rugged, savanna-covered islands between Flores and Sumbawa, home to the only place on Earth where Komodo dragons still roam wild.

The park's islands are as visually striking as its dragons — Padar's three-bayed viewpoint, Pink Beach's rose-tinted sand, and turquoise water that draws divers for some of Indonesia's richest reefs outside Raja Ampat.

Labuan Bajo, the harbour town on Flores that serves as the park's gateway, has grown fast in recent years, and Flores itself holds further rewards beyond the harbour — not least Kelimutu, a volcano with three crater lakes that change colour over time.

whyVisit.intro: Komodo and Flores' case rests on wild wildlife and island scenery found almost nowhere else on Earth.

points.title: Komodo dragons are found wild nowhere else
points.text: This is the only place on the planet these giant monitor lizards still live in their natural habitat.

points.title: Padar Island's viewpoint is one of Indonesia's iconic views
points.text: Three curved bays of different coloured sand visible from a single hilltop, especially striking at sunrise.

points.title: Pink Beach is a rare natural phenomenon
points.text: Its sand gets its rose tint from crushed red coral mixed with white sand, one of only a handful of such beaches worldwide.

points.title: The diving is world-class
points.text: Strong currents feed the park's reefs, drawing manta rays and dense marine life close to the surface.

points.title: Kelimutu adds an entirely different landscape
points.text: Three crater lakes on Flores that shift colour over months and years, a unique geological phenomenon.

attractionsIntro: Most of Komodo's essential sights are reached only by boat, making a multi-day trip the standard way to see them properly.

attractions.name: Padar Island Viewpoint

image.file: File:Padar Island, Komodo National Park, Indonesia, 20250822 0913 2640.jpg
image.alt: The three-bayed viewpoint from the top of Padar Island

attractions.text: One of Indonesia's most photographed views, a short but steep climb rewarded with three curved bays of black, white and pink sand spread below.
attractions.tip: Arrive at sunrise, both for the light and to beat the heat of the climb.

attractions.name: Pink Beach

image.file: File:Pink Beach, Padar Island, Komodo National Park, Indonesia, 20250822 1108 2680.jpg
image.alt: The rose-tinted sand of Pink Beach in Komodo National Park

attractions.text: A rare rose-tinted beach, its colour coming from crushed red coral mixed into the white sand, with excellent snorkelling just offshore.
attractions.tip: The pink tint shows best when the sand is wet, right at the waterline.

attractions.name: Komodo Island

image.alt: A wild Komodo dragon on Komodo Island

attractions.text: The original home of the Komodo dragon, with ranger-guided walking trails offering a real chance of spotting these giant lizards wild.
attractions.tip: Rangers carry forked sticks for safety — always stay close to your guide.

attractions.name: Rinca Island

image.alt: Komodo dragons resting on Rinca Island

attractions.text: Offering a higher dragon-sighting chance than Komodo island itself, with a shorter, easier ranger-led walking trail.
attractions.tip: Dragons often rest near the ranger station kitchen — sightings here are almost guaranteed.

attractions.name: Labuan Bajo

image.alt: Boats moored in the harbour at Labuan Bajo, Flores

attractions.text: The fast-growing gateway town to Komodo National Park, its harbour packed with liveaboard boats and a lively sunset waterfront.
attractions.tip: The waterfront restaurants along the harbour are the best spot for a sunset dinner.

attractions.name: Kelimutu Crater Lakes

image.alt: The three coloured crater lakes of Kelimutu volcano in Flores

attractions.text: A unique volcanic phenomenon further into Flores, three crater lakes side by side that shift between different colours over months and years.
attractions.tip: It's a long drive from Labuan Bajo — most visitors fly into or out of nearby Ende or Maumere instead.

attractions.name: Manta Point

image.alt: A giant manta ray gliding through the water

attractions.text: A reliable manta ray cleaning station within the park, drawing these giant rays close enough for excellent snorkelling and diving.
attractions.tip: Boat trips time visits around tidal currents — ask your operator about the best window.

thingsToDoIntro: A Komodo trip revolves around boat-based island-hopping, mixing wildlife, beaches and diving over several days.

thingsToDo.title: Hike Padar Island at sunrise

image.file: File:Padar Island, Komodo National Park, Indonesia, 20250822 0908 2631.jpg
image.alt: Early morning light over Padar Island's viewpoint

thingsToDo.text: An essential Komodo experience, climbing to the viewpoint before the heat and crowds of midday.
thingsToDo.tip: Liveaboards often anchor overnight nearby specifically for an early Padar climb.

thingsToDo.title: See wild Komodo dragons with a ranger

image.alt: A Komodo dragon walking through dry grassland on Rinca Island

thingsToDo.text: An unforgettable wildlife encounter, walking within safe but close distance of the world's largest living lizard.
thingsToDo.tip: Early morning tours see dragons more active before the day's heat sets in.

thingsToDo.title: Snorkel or dive with manta rays

image.alt: A snorkeller close to a manta ray underwater

thingsToDo.text: A thrilling encounter at the park's manta cleaning stations, where these giant rays circle close to the surface.
thingsToDo.tip: A wetsuit is worth renting even for snorkelling — currents here can be strong and cool.

thingsToDo.title: Relax on Pink Beach

image.file: File:Pink Beach, Padar Island, Komodo National Park, Indonesia, 20250822 1108 2683.jpg
image.alt: The rose-tinted sand and clear water of Pink Beach

thingsToDo.text: A worthwhile stop on any island-hopping itinerary, with good snorkelling right off the beach itself.
thingsToDo.tip: Bring reef-safe sunscreen — the beach sits within a protected marine park.

thingsToDo.title: Island-hop by liveaboard boat

image.file: File:Typical boats with couches that take tourists to different islands (17118151282).jpg
image.alt: A traditional wooden liveaboard boat used for island-hopping in Komodo

thingsToDo.text: The classic way to see Komodo properly, sleeping aboard a traditional wooden phinisi boat over two or three days.
thingsToDo.tip: Book a few months ahead in peak season — good boats fill up fast.

thingsToDo.title: Watch sunset in Labuan Bajo

image.alt: Sunset over the harbour at Labuan Bajo

thingsToDo.text: A relaxed way to end a day of island-hopping, with harbourside bars and restaurants facing directly into the sunset.
thingsToDo.tip: Rooftop bars along the hillside above the harbour give the best elevated sunset views.

foodIntro: Flores' food is centred on fresh seafood, reflecting Labuan Bajo's identity as a working fishing harbour turned dive hub.

foods.name: Ikan bakar (grilled fish)

image.alt: Ikan bakar, grilled fish, a common Indonesian coastal dish

foods.text: The standard evening meal along the Labuan Bajo waterfront, whole fish grilled over charcoal and served with rice and sambal.
foods.whereToTry: Waterfront restaurants along Labuan Bajo's harbour.

foods.name: Sambal

image.file: File:SAMBAL - The must have chili dipping.jpg
image.alt: A bowl of sambal, Indonesian chili sauce

foods.text: An essential condiment at every meal, a fiery chili sauce that varies noticeably from restaurant to restaurant.
foods.whereToTry: Alongside nearly every meal throughout Flores.

foods.name: Nasi goreng

image.alt: A plate of nasi goreng, Indonesian fried rice, topped with a fried egg

foods.text: A reliable option aboard liveaboard boats and at harbourside warungs alike.
foods.whereToTry: Warungs and liveaboard boat kitchens throughout the region.

foods.name: Flores coffee

image.alt: Roasted coffee beans, grown across Flores' volcanic highlands

foods.text: Grown across Flores' volcanic highlands, particularly around Bajawa, with a distinct, full-bodied character.
foods.whereToTry: Cafés in Labuan Bajo and highland towns further into Flores.

foods.name: Jagung titi
foods.text: A traditional Flores snack, corn kernels hand-flattened and toasted, often eaten alongside coffee.
foods.whereToTry: Markets and warungs in Flores' highland towns.

foods.name: Fresh seafood catch
foods.text: Landed daily at Labuan Bajo's harbour, with the day's catch often visible right at the fish market each morning.
foods.whereToTry: The fish market and harbourside restaurants in Labuan Bajo.

accommodation.intro: Most visitors base themselves in Labuan Bajo, or sleep aboard a liveaboard boat for the park itself.

areas.name: Labuan Bajo
areas.bestFor: The genuine gateway town, with the widest range of hotels
areas.text: Ranges from budget guesthouses to hillside resorts overlooking the harbour.

areas.name: Liveaboard boat
areas.bestFor: Seeing the park's islands properly over multiple days
areas.text: The classic way to explore Komodo, sleeping aboard between island stops.

gettingThere.intro: Labuan Bajo is reached almost exclusively by air, with Komodo National Park itself accessible only by boat.

options.text: The standard way in, with direct flights from Bali, Jakarta and other major Indonesian cities.
options.detail: Komodo Airport sits just outside the town centre.

options.mode: Liveaboard or day boat from Labuan Bajo
options.text: The only way to reach Komodo National Park's islands themselves.
options.detail: Boats depart from Labuan Bajo's harbour daily in season.

options.mode: Onward flight to Ende or Maumere for Kelimutu
options.text: The practical way to reach Kelimutu without a very long overland drive from Labuan Bajo.
options.detail: Short regional flights connect these towns within Flores.

gettingAround.intro: Getting around Komodo National Park means boats — there are no roads connecting its islands.

options.text: The best way to see multiple islands without backtracking to Labuan Bajo each night.
options.detail: Typically booked for 2-4 days, visiting several islands and dive sites.

options.text: Suit visitors with less time, covering one or two islands in a single day from Labuan Bajo.
options.detail: Shared and private options are both widely available.

options.mode: Car or scooter within Labuan Bajo
options.text: Useful for getting around the town itself and to the airport.
options.detail: Ride-hailing apps have more limited coverage here than in Bali or Java.

bestTime.headline: April to December for calmer seas and easier boat access
bestTime.summary: Dry season brings calmer water for island-hopping, though visibility for diving actually peaks slightly later in the year.

seasons.text: The most reliable weather and calmest seas for boat-based island-hopping.
Often the best diving visibility of the year, with generally still-manageable seas.
Rougher seas can disrupt boat trips, and some operators reduce their schedules.
Workable year-round, though the crater lakes can be shrouded in mist at any time of year.

bestTime.avoid: Avoid booking a tight liveaboard schedule deep in wet season (January–March), when rough seas most often disrupt boat plans.

tipsIntro: A handful of practical notes make a Komodo trip go far more smoothly.
tips: Book a reputable boat operator — safety standards vary noticeably between companies.
Bring reef-safe sunscreen, required within the marine park.
Never approach Komodo dragons without a ranger present.
Pack seasickness medication if prone to it — open-water crossings can get rough.
Book liveaboards months ahead for peak dry-season dates.
Bring cash — card payments are limited outside Labuan Bajo's main hotels.

faq.q: Is it safe to see Komodo dragons in the wild?
faq.a: Yes, with a park ranger present at all times — never attempt to see them without one.

faq.q: How do you get to Komodo National Park?
faq.a: Fly into Labuan Bajo on Flores, then take a boat — there's no other way into the park itself.

faq.q: Is Komodo Island or Rinca Island better for seeing dragons?
faq.a: Rinca offers a slightly higher sighting chance with an easier walk, though both islands are worthwhile.

faq.q: How many days do you need for Komodo National Park?
faq.a: Two to four days covers the park's highlights, whether as day trips from Labuan Bajo or a short liveaboard.

faq.q: Is Pink Beach's sand really pink?
faq.a: Yes, though subtly — the rose tint comes from crushed red coral mixed into white sand, and shows best when wet.

faq.q: Can you combine Komodo with Kelimutu on Flores?
faq.a: Yes, though it typically requires a separate regional flight to Ende or Maumere, since it's a long overland drive from Labuan Bajo.
